folds.title: The AI's 2 questions
folds.html:
• Question 1, as asked: "Does the employer that wrote this posting deliver goods, run routes, dispatch drivers or technicians, keep a fleet of vehicles for delivering goods or for visits to customers, or send workers out to customers to install, repair, service, pick up or deliver things? It counts when it does this with people or vehicles it employs or directs, or when it delivers its own goods to its customers or between its own sites through outside freight or parcel carriers or delivery partners that it chooses, schedules or manages. Carrying passengers is not delivering goods." (not said, no, yes)
  • What would the person hired mainly do? (other; software or data; warehouse or store; field technician; fleet management; delivery operations management; dispatch or routing; driving or courier)
  • For question 1, it also picks the line of the posting that shows it. Code copies that line word for word as the quote.
  • An answer counts as sure when the model gives it 80 percent or more. An unsure answer sends the company to a person only when the job could still qualify for Brief ready (new, not seasonal, not a repost, not outside the US, and not already a sure "no"). An unsure answer is never shown as a fact.
  • I wrote questions 1 and 2 after reading these boards' job titles, and some examples in them come from these postings (junk removal, medical waste pick-up, towing, a delivery station, DOT compliance). Version 2 reworded question 1 (carriers count, passengers do not) and question 2's management and dispatch options, after version 1's results were seen. Its words "freight or parcel carriers" echo the Director of Home Delivery posting, and its 60-day window for leadership roles and its narrower rule for unsure answers came from reviews of version 1's results on that posting and on a training-design job.
  • Version 1, on 30 practice postings from other companies: a third question (who makes the deliveries) was tested and cut, and the quote cutoff moved from 50 to 20 percent. Version 2, on a new draw of 30: question 1 was reworded once, then sat exactly at two of my limits (sure but wrong on 3 of 30, all shipping postings; changed on 3 of 30 with the answer options reversed). The README has the details.

folds.title: The rules
folds.html:
• A delivery job title holds one of these words: delivery, deliveries, delivering, dispatch, dispatcher(s), driver(s), courier(s), fleet(s), last mile, logistics, transportation, routing, route(s), field technician(s), field service technician(s). A delivery job with none of them in its title is never read.
  • The title rule (no AI) treats version 2's new title words like "delivery", except that a title with "analyst" counts as not delivery work and a field technician counts as delivery work unless the department is technical.
  • New means the job has a posting from the last 30 days, or 60 days for a leadership title (manager, director, head of). Leadership jobs are read first. A job counts as an old one reposted when any of its postings, anywhere at the company, is over 90 days old. I chose these two cutoffs.
  • A job is one company plus one job title. Reposts of the same title count once, and anything after a dash or bracket is ignored. Two different titles for the same job count as two jobs.
  • The AI reads one posting per job: its newest posting in the United States, or its newest posting when none is in the US. At most 8 jobs per company, leadership jobs first.
  • Dates clustered: a board of 20 or more postings where four in five show dates no more than 14 days apart.
  • Seasonal: a title that says seasonal, holiday, temporary or peak, or a set phrase in the text such as "seasonal position".
  • Region: the United States, checked per posting. That is my choice, not Nash's.
  • One board (Carvana's) also lists jobs for a second business that does different work; a rule I wrote for that board after reading it leaves those out.
  • A board is shown only when I can confirm whose it is: the board states the company's name, or at least 3 of its postings do.

folds.title: How each company is sorted, in order
folds.html:
1. Needs a person, DATES CLUSTERED: on a board of 20 or more postings, four in five or more show dates no more than 14 days apart.
  2. Needs a person, NOT READ: a new job's posting could not be read, or the line the AI picked is not in it.
  3. Brief ready: a new job that the AI was sure is delivery, dispatch or fleet work at a company that runs it, in the United States, not seasonal, and not an old job reposted.
  4. Needs a person, PLACE UNCLEAR: a new job the AI was sure is delivery work, but its place cannot be read (for example only "Remote").
  5. Needs a person, AI UNSURE: the AI was unsure on a new job that could still qualify.
  6. Skipped, with the first reason that is true:
    • the AI read every job as other work;
    • the postings do not show the company running its own deliveries;
    • every new job is an old one reposted;
    • the only new jobs are seasonal;
    • no job is in the United States, or its place could not be read;
    • open a while: the newest posting for a job the AI was sure is delivery work is 31 to 90 days old;
    • nothing new: no new job, and the newest job the AI was sure about is older than that, or there is none;
    • no new job qualifies: there is a new job, but each one is outside the US, seasonal, a repost, or not read as delivery work at this company.
  7. Needs a person, NO RULE FITS: none of the above. The step before always applies when a new job exists, so this one cannot be reached; it stays as a guard.

folds.title: How the list of boards was made
folds.html:
• While planning, 1,931 company names were tried on three job-board systems (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby). Most were not found. The boards found were checked one at a time, and 71 were kept. The list is not complete.
  • Only those three systems are read. A company that posts jobs only on its own careers site or on another system is never seen.
  • Only public postings were read, slowly and without logging in. The page shows only short quotes.
  • The posting text was read by the AI model, and by the AI assistants and the second AI that wrote and checked the answer key.
  • I left out the companies I could find that Nash names in public. For the 21 companies shown, who owns each was also looked up; none is owned by one of those companies. Five owners could not be fully confirmed, and for the 1-800-GOT-JUNK board only the brand's owner was looked up, not the franchise group that runs it. I can't see the rest of Nash's customers.
  • Delivery and courier companies themselves are left off the list.
  • Each company's market is my label, from one public Nash industry page. Nash's own labels would replace mine. The label does not affect which group a company is in.
